propositions.text: Applicant is a DRC citizen seeking judicial review of RPD decision dismissing refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Mr. Kamwanga, is a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (the DRC). He seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (the RPD) dated February 1, 2018 dismissing his claim for refugee protection (the Decision).

propositions.text: RPD rejected Applicant's testimony based on adverse credibility findings and found he is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected the Applicant’s testimony based on adverse credibility findings and concluded that the Applicant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a DRC citizen seeking judicial review of the RPD decision dismissing his refugee claim due to adverse credibility findings.

propositions.text: Application will be allowed despite no procedural fairness breach by RPD.
propositions.quote: As explained below, the application will be allowed. While I have found no breach of procedural fairness on the part of the RPD,

propositions.text: RPD member failed to justify credibility conclusions per Vavilov review framework.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicant that the member failed to justify their credibility conclusions with reasons that respond to the review framework established in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 (Vavilov).

paragraphs.summary: The court will allow the application, finding no procedural fairness breach but that the RPD failed to justify credibility conclusions per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Applicant fears imprisonment and death by DRC authorities due to Church membership since 2005.
propositions.quote: The Applicant fears being imprisoned and killed by governmental authorities in the DRC because he has been a member of the Église Ministère de la Restauration à partir de l’Afrique Noire (the Church) since 2005.

propositions.text: Church leader Mukungubila denounced President Kabila's regime; government targeted Church members.
propositions.quote: The Church’s leader, Paul Joseph Mukungubila Mutombo is a politician who denounced the regime of President Kabila. The Church was targeted by the government’s intelligence authorities, culminating in events in late December 2013 when the authorities began arresting members of the Church.

propositions.text: Government blamed Church for violence after December 2013 protests, forcing Mukungubila to flee to South Africa.
propositions.quote: In response, Church members held a protest against the government on December 30, 2013. The Applicant alleges that the government then staged a number of violent incidents in the country and blamed the Church for the violence, forcing Mr. Mukungubila to flee to South Africa.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges fearing imprisonment and death due to Church membership; government targeted Church and blamed it for violence, forcing leader to flee.

propositions.text: Government broadened arrests to regular Church members by February 2014; Applicant fled to brother's home in Likasi.
propositions.quote: The Applicant states that the government initially arrested senior Church members but, by February 2014, had broadened its operations to target other, regular members of the Church. At this point, the Applicant became afraid for his own safety in Lubumbashi where he lived and went to stay with his older brother in Likasi in the DRC.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant states government expanded arrests to regular Church members by Feb 2014, prompting him to flee to brother's home in Likasi.

propositions.text: Applicant's timeline of events from Dec 2013 to April 2016 details arrests, escapes, movements, and refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The timeline of critical events as recounted in the Applicant’s Basis of Claim form (BOC) is as follows: December 28, 2013: Government authorities arrested Church members for distributing a letter written by Mr. Mukungubila. December 29, 2013: One Church member died during a confrontation with government authorities at the Church. The Applicant was not present at the Church that day. December 30, 2013: Church members protested and the government responded by staging attacks at prominent state buildings and facilities around the country. The government blamed the Church for the attacks and resulting chaos and began a campaign of arresting senior Church members. February 2014 (approx.): The Applicant learned that the government had begun to target regular members of the Church, left Lubumbashi, and went to live with his brother in Likasi. March 2014: The Applicant feared staying too long in one place and moved to his parent’s home in Lubumbashi. There, he was arrested by members of the DRC’s intelligence authority, deprived of food and toilet facilities, beaten and threatened with death, all while being pressured for information concerning the Church. July 1, 2014: The Applicant escaped his captors with the assistance of his uncle, a former intelligence agent. The Applicant returned to his brother’s house in Likasi and remained hidden in the house. December 2, 2014: The Applicant was again arrested and detained by the security authorities who continued the government’s operations against Church members. July 28, 2015: The Applicant escaped captivity with the assistance of his uncle. The uncle informed the Applicant he could not stay at his home and the Applicant moved to a remote northern village. March 2, 2016: The Applicant traveled to Zambia for an interview to obtain a U.S. visa to attend a religious conference in the United States. He then returned to the DRC. March 21, 2016: The Applicant left the DRC for the United States. April 2016: The Applicant traveled to the Canadian border and made a refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's Basis of Claim form details timeline of arrests, escapes, movements, and refugee claim from Dec 2013 to April 2016.

propositions.text: RPD heard claim Oct 26, 2017 and issued Decision Feb 1, 2018; judicial review held pending Kreishan decisions.
propositions.quote: The RPD heard the Applicant’s claim on October 26, 2017 and issued the Decision on February 1, 2018. This application for judicial review was held in abeyance pending the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Kreishan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FCA 223, and the appeal of that decision to the Supreme Court of Canada (leave to appeal dismissed on March 5, 2020).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RPD heard the claim in 2017, issued decision in 2018, and judicial review was held pending Kreishan appeals.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicant's testimony not credible and did not establish basis for fear of persecution or serious harm.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Applicant’s testimony was not credible and concluded that he had not established the allegations that formed the basis of his fear of persecution and serious harm in the DRC.

propositions.text: RPD identified three issues in Applicant's testimony.
propositions.quote: The RPD identified three issues in the Applicant’s testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Applicant's testimony not credible and identified three issues in his testimony.

propositions.text: RPD questioned why Applicant delayed fleeing to brother's home after Dec 2013 incidents, returned after jail escape, and returned to DRC after Zambia interview.
propositions.quote: The RPD questioned why the Applicant: did not flee to his brother’s home in Likasi immediately after the December 30, 2013 incidents at the Church; returned to his brother’s house after his first escape from jail in July 2014; travelled back to the DRC after his interview in early March 2016 at the U.S. embassy in Zambia.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicant's failure to explain conduct damaged his credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Applicant had not provided reasonable explanations to their questions and that his failure to explain his conduct damaged his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD questioned Applicant's conduct and found his failure to explain it damaged his credibility.

propositions.text: RPD considered documentary evidence but found it lacked probative value to restore credibility.
propositions.quote: The RPD then considered the Applicant’s documentary evidence: a letter from the Centre international de formation en droits humain et développement dated July 25, 2015 (the Letter); various documents pertaining to his brother’s successful refugee claim in South Africa; and, a series of emails between himself and family members. The RPD found that the documents lacked sufficient probative value to re-establish the Applicant’s credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Applicant's documentary evidence lacked probative value to restore his credibility.

propositions.text: Applicant alleges RPD breached procedural fairness by not allowing response to documentary evidence concerns during hearing.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the RPD breached his right to procedural fairness because he was not provided an opportunity to respond during the hearing to the tribunal’s concerns with his documentary evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RPD should assess documents on their face without authenticity concerns and not assign low probative value.
propositions.quote: Having failed to raise any issues it had with his supporting documents at the hearing, the Applicant states that the RPD was required to assess the documents on what they say and, in the absence of authenticity concerns, could not ascribe them little probative value.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges the RPD breached procedural fairness by not allowing response to documentary concerns and improperly assigning low probative value.

propositions.text: Breach of procedural fairness allegations resemble correctness standard; court determines fairness in all circumstances.
propositions.quote: Allegations of breach of procedural fairness do not necessarily lend themselves to a standard of review analysis, although the Court’s approach to such allegations resembles that of correctness (Canadian Pacific Railway v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 (Canadian Pacific)). The role of the Court is to determine whether the procedure is fair in all the circumstances (Canadian Pacific at paras 54–56; Alkhoury v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 153 at para 10).

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness breach allegations resemble correctness standard; court assesses fairness in all circumstances.

propositions.text: Court finds no procedural fairness breach by RPD in assessing Applicant's documents.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded by the Applicant’s arguments and find that the RPD committed no breach of procedural fairness in assessing the documents submitted for its consideration by the Applicant.

propositions.text: Respondent argues RPD must consider and weigh evidence in refugee claims.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that the RPD is required to consider the evidence provided by a refugee claimant and to weigh that evidence in relation to the claim under scrutiny.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel invited RPD to review documents and argued they support credibility; Applicant cannot be surprised by RPD's review.
propositions.quote: I note that the Applicant’s counsel invited the RPD to review the documents in question during the hearing and argued that they support the Applicant’s credibility. The Applicant cannot now be surprised that the RPD reviewed the documents in its assessment of his refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no procedural fairness breach; Respondent says RPD must weigh evidence; Applicant invited RPD to review documents.

propositions.text: RPD gave reasons for rejecting testimony and assessed documents' probative value without authenticity concerns; no procedural error.
propositions.quote: In the Decision, the RPD set out its reasons for rejecting the Applicant’s testimony based on lack of credibility and turned to the supporting documents. As the Applicant notes, the RPD raised no concern as to the authenticity of the documents. Where relevant to the individual document, the RPD considered their probative value, whether the facts set out were sufficient to establish one or more elements of the Applicant’s claim, the weight or persuasiveness of the documents, and their sufficiency in re-establishing the Applicant’s allegations (see, Magonza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 14 at paras 21-35; Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Sellan, 2008 FCA 381 at para 3). In so doing, the RPD committed no procedural error.

propositions.text: Applicant's arguments about document analysis are challenges to reasonableness, not procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s arguments regarding the member’s analysis of his documents and the country documentation are better viewed as arguments contesting the reasonableness of that analysis and not the fairness of the RPD’s process.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD gave reasons rejecting testimony and assessed documents properly; Applicant's arguments challenge reasonableness, not fairness.

propositions.text: Determinative issue is whether RPD's credibility reasons and negative conclusions are reasonable.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this application is whether the RPD’s reasons and negative conclusions regarding the Applicant’s credibility are reasonable.

propositions.text: Credibility issue challenges merits and must be reviewed for reasonableness per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The parties submit, and I agree, that this issue challenges the merits of the Decision and must be reviewed for reasonableness (Vavilov at paras 10, 25).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the key issue is whether RPD's credibility conclusions are reasonable, reviewed under Vavilov standard.

propositions.text: Applicant argues RPD's adverse credibility conclusion is unreasonable and over-zealous, and failed to analyze section 97 claim separately.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that (1) the RPD’s conclusion that his testimony was not credible is not reasonable and reflects an over-zealous assessment of his evidence against the central elements of his claim; and (2) the RPD erred in failing to conduct a separate analysis of his claim under section 97.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD's adverse credibility conclusion is unreasonable and failed to analyze section 97 claim separately.

propositions.text: Respondent contends RPD's statement means it did not believe Applicant was a Church member.
propositions.quote: The Respondent’s contention is that the RPD’s general statement that the Applicant had not credibly established his allegations must be read to mean that the tribunal did not believe he was a Church member.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent contends RPD's statement means it did not believe Applicant was a Church member.

propositions.text: RPD made no finding on Applicant's Church membership; statement about membership insufficient to conclude rejection of membership.
propositions.quote: The RPD makes no finding in the Decision regarding the Applicant’s membership in the Church. In response to a question from counsel during the hearing, the RPD indicated that its credibility concerns included the issue of membership. Nevertheless, I find that this statement, in the absence of specific reference to the issue, is not sufficient to read the RPD’s rejection of the Applicant’s “allegations” as a finding that he was not a member of the Church.

propositions.text: RPD's analysis focused on specific credibility findings; general references to allegations should be read in context.
propositions.quote: The RPD centred its analysis of credibility on specific findings and the introductory and closing references in the Decision to the Applicant’s allegations are properly read in the context of the findings made.

propositions.text: If RPD concluded Applicant was not Church member, it was not done transparently or intelligibly.
propositions.quote: Indeed, if the Decision is read as premised on a conclusion that the Applicant was not a Church member, there is little doubt that such conclusion was not made transparently or intelligibly.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RPD made no clear finding on Church membership; any rejection of membership was not transparent or intelligible.

propositions.text: Applicant's challenge to RPD's adverse credibility findings as implausibility findings is rejected; RPD made no implausibility finding.
propositions.quote: There is a distinction between a negative credibility finding and a finding that a claimant’s narrative of one or more events is implausible. The RPD made no reference in the Decision to implausibility and the Applicant has not persuaded me that the way in which the adverse findings were made denotes a conclusion that his version of events was not plausible.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Applicant's argument that adverse credibility findings were implausibility findings; RPD made no implausibility finding.

propositions.text: RPD's reasons for rejecting testimony lack transparency and coherent reasoning per Vavilov para 85.
propositions.quote: I do, however, agree with the Applicant that the RPD’s reasons for rejecting the Applicant’s testimony are not transparent when viewed against the record and do not reflect a coherent chain of reasoning that justifies its conclusions (Vavilov at para 85).

propositions.text: Conclusion based primarily on two of RPD's credibility findings.
propositions.quote: I base my conclusion primarily on two of the RPD’s credibility findings.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees RPD's reasons rejecting testimony lack transparency and coherent reasoning, based on two credibility findings.

propositions.text: RPD questioned why Applicant returned to brother's house after jail escape and did not make other arrangements.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the Applicant returned to his brother’s house after his escape from jail in July 2014 and asked why he thought government authorities could not find him in Likasi.

propositions.text: RPD did not accept Applicant's explanation that March 2014 arrest was at parents' home, not Likasi.
propositions.quote: The member did not accept the Applicant’s explanation that he had been arrested from his parents’ home in Lubumbashi in March 2014, and not in Likasi.

propositions.text: RPD expected Applicant to make other arrangements; failure damaged credibility of March 2014 arrest allegation.
propositions.quote: The RPD stated that it would have expected the Applicant to make other arrangements and that his failure to do so damaged the credibility of his alleged arrest in March 2014.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Applicant's return to brother's house after jail escape and failure to make other arrangements damaged credibility of March 2014 arrest.

propositions.text: The RPD's reasoning is not intelligible and vague regarding the Applicant's return to his brother's house.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD’s reasoning is not intelligible. The RPD stated that “[i]n light of his other allegations”, the Applicant had not provided a reasonable explanation for returning to his brother’s house.

propositions.text: The RPD ignored the substance of the Applicant's evidence about his fear and arrest history in Lubumbashi.
propositions.quote: The RPD relied on the Applicant’s testimony that he returned to Lubumbashi because he was afraid of staying too long in one place to conclude that he was aware of the risk of staying at his brother’s home. The conclusion ignores the substance of the Applicant’s evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant was arrested at his parents' home in Lubumbashi on March 1, 2014; no evidence security tracked him to brother's home in Likasi.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was arrested at his parents’ home in Lubumbashi on March 1, 2014. There is no evidence in the record that the security authorities had knowledge of his older brother’s home in Likasi or that they had tracked the Applicant to Likasi.

propositions.text: Applicant remained hidden at brother's house after initial arrest due to awareness of heightened risk.
propositions.quote: In addition, the Applicant remained hidden in the house after his initial arrest because he was aware of the heightened risk.

propositions.text: RPD gave no convincing argument why Applicant should have made alternate arrangements instead of staying at brother's home.
propositions.quote: In my view, the RPD provided no convincing argument for its conclusion that it would have expected the Applicant to make alternate arrangements.

propositions.text: Respondent argues RPD based conclusion on Applicant's arrest at one family home and unreasonableness of hiding at another family member's home.
propositions.quote: The Respondent’s argument that the RPD based its conclusion on the fact that the Applicant had been arrested at one family home and could not reasonably expect to remain hidden at the home of another family member is not reflected in the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's reasoning about the Applicant's return to his brother's house vague and ignoring key evidence; the Respondent's argument is not reflected in the Decision.

propositions.text: RPD asked Applicant to explain return to DRC after March 2016 US embassy interview in Zambia.
propositions.quote: The RPD asked the Applicant to explain why he returned to the DRC after his interview in early March 2016 at the U.S. embassy in Zambia.

propositions.text: Applicant explained he planned to travel to US with a group and had to return to DRC pending group's departure.
propositions.quote: The Applicant explained that he was planning to travel to the United States with a group and that he had had no choice but to return to the DRC pending the group’s departure later the same month.

propositions.text: Applicant stated his uncle instructed him to return because uncle could provide security in Lubumbashi.
propositions.quote: He also stated that his uncle had instructed him to return because the uncle could provide security in Lubumbashi.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicant did not provide reasonable explanation for reavailment to DRC and that return damaged credibility about government pursuit.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Applicant had not provided a reasonable explanation for his reavailment to the DRC. In its view, the Applicant’s return further damaged his credibility with regard to whether he was being sought by the government.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD asked why the Applicant returned to DRC after a US embassy interview; the Applicant explained travel plans and uncle's security offer, but RPD found explanation unreasonable and damaging to credibility.

propositions.text: RPD discounted Applicant's explanation with little consideration of his need to travel with the group.
propositions.quote: The RPD discounts the Applicant’s explanation for his return to the DRC with little consideration of his need to travel with the group.

propositions.text: RPD's reliance on country documentation about Church members fleeing to Zambia fails to engage with Applicant's specific reason for return.
propositions.quote: The RPD’s reliance on the fact that the country documentation indicated that many members of the Church had fled to Zambia at the time fails to engage with the Applicant’s specific reason for his course of action.

propositions.text: RPD failed to consider short duration of Applicant's reavailment to DRC.
propositions.quote: The RPD also failed to consider the short duration of the reavailment.

propositions.text: Applicant's lack of intention to remain in DRC and quick departure are material facts relevant to credibility (Abawaji v Canada).
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not intend to return to the DRC and remain there for any appreciable period of time (Abawaji v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1065 at para 15).

propositions.text: Absence of intention to remain and quick departure should have been part of RPD's analysis but were omitted.
propositions.quote: The absence of an intention to remain in the DRC coupled with the Applicant’s departure from the country soon after his return were material factual aspects that should reasonably have formed part of the RPD’s analysis.

propositions.text: There are material omissions in RPD's assessment of Applicant's brief return to DRC pending US departure.
propositions.quote: As a result, I find that there are material omissions in the RPD’s assessment of the Applicant’s brief return to the DRC pending his departure for the United States.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD failed to properly consider the Applicant's travel needs, short return duration, and intention not to remain in DRC, omitting material facts in its assessment.

propositions.text: Errors in RPD's credibility assessment are significant and require redetermination of refugee claim (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: The foregoing errors in the RPD’s assessment of the Applicant’s credibility are significant shortcomings in the Decision and require redetermination of his refugee claim (Vavilov at para 100).

propositions.text: No reviewable error in RPD's analysis of Applicant's delay fleeing to brother's home after December 2013 incidents.
propositions.quote: I note that the RPD’s first credibility concern centred on the Applicant’s delay in fleeing to his brother’s home in Likasi after the December 30, 2013 incidents at the Church and I find no reviewable error in this aspect of the RPD’s analysis.

propositions.text: Overall credibility assessment by RPD is undermined by errors discussed in judgment.
propositions.quote: However, the overall assessment of the Applicant’s credibility by the RPD is undermined by the errors discussed in this judgment.

propositions.text: RPD's ultimate conclusion rejecting Applicant's allegations rests on cumulative reasons for rejecting testimony.
propositions.quote: It is evident from the Decision that the member’s ultimate conclusion that the Applicant had not established his allegations rests on their cumulative reasons for rejecting his testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds significant errors in the RPD's credibility assessment requiring redetermination, though no error on delay fleeing to brother's home; overall credibility is undermined.

propositions.text: RPD could reasonably conclude documentary evidence was insufficient to overcome credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: Briefly, I find that the RPD could reasonably conclude that the documentary evidence submitted by the Applicant was not sufficient to overcome its credibility concerns.

propositions.text: Lack of credibility on central refugee claim elements may apply to documentary evidence corroborating facts (Abdelgadir v Canada).
propositions.quote: Moreover, a lack of credibility with respect to the central elements of a refugee claim may apply to documentary evidence adduced to corroborate a version of the facts (Abdelgadir v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 721 para 18).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD reasonably concluded documentary evidence was insufficient to overcome credibility concerns, citing precedent on credibility and documentary evidence.

propositions.text: RPD did not err in failing to undertake separate section 97 analysis; lack of credibility suffices to reject claim under sections 96 and 97 unless independent credible evidence exists.
propositions.quote: Finally, although I have concluded that the RPD’s credibility analysis is neither transparent nor justified, the RPD did not err in failing to undertake a separate section 97 analysis of the Applicant’s evidence. A finding that an applicant lacks credibility is sufficient to justify the rejection of a refugee claim under both sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record to support a section 97 decision (Qahramanloei v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 422 at para 28; Zamor v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 672 at para 8).

propositions.text: Applicant relied on same facts and evidence for both section 96 and section 97 claims.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Applicant relied on the same facts and evidence in respect of his section 96 and section 97 claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD did not err by not separately analyzing section 97 claims, as lack of credibility suffices absent independent credible evidence; Applicant used same evidence for both claims.

propositions.text: Application is allowed and Applicant's refugee claim is returned to an independent RPD panel for redetermination.
propositions.quote: The application is allowed and the Applicant’s refugee claim returned to an independent panel of the RPD for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the application and returns the Applicant's refugee claim to an independent RPD panel for redetermination.

propositions.text: No question for certification was proposed or arises in this case.
propositions.quote: No question for certification was proposed by the parties and none arises in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no question for certification was proposed or arises in this case.
